summary: Defines a content media feature schema for Internet fax, a way to describe the capabilities of a fax device and the features of a document. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sending a fax, one machine has to say what it can handle: black and white or colour, what resolution, which coding, what paper. This document defines the words for those answers, using the general media feature syntax so that fax is not the only thing that can use them. Two machines can then compare what one can send with what the other can receive, and agree on a format without guessing.

questions: what is the internet fax feature schema
how do fax machines describe their capabilities
what is mrc in internet fax
subtitle: A common vocabulary for fax systems to say what they can handle, so a sender can pick a format the receiver will accept.

tldr.problem: A fax sender needs to know what the receiving fax system can actually handle: which image coding, which resolution, which paper size, how much colour. Without a shared vocabulary, the two ends have to guess.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a profile of the media feature registration and syntax mechanisms, and lists the feature tags that extended Internet fax systems recognise: size, resolution, media type, paper size, colour capability, colour model, image coding and the MRC features, with the registrations for the fax-specific tags in its appendix.
tldr.outcome: Two systems can then compare a description of what they can do with a description of what they have, and work out the best format to send, as the worked examples show. The feature tags are registered in the IETF tree, and the document adds one new tag, color-illuminant.

today: RFC 2879 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2000. It replaced RFC 2531 with a second version of the schema, registering the fax feature tags in the IETF tree and adding one new tag, color-illuminant. It is a profile of the media feature mechanisms in RFC 2506 and RFC 2533, and it does not specify how capability information is exchanged.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines a content media feature schema for Internet fax. It is a profile of the media feature registration mechanisms for use in performing capability identification between extended Internet fax systems, and it replaces and updates the feature schema defined in RFC 2531.

The media feature description mechanisms do not describe any specific mechanism for communicating capability information, but they do presume that any such mechanism will transfer textual values. Together with this feature schema, they specify a textual format for describing Internet fax capability information. The range of capabilities that can be indicated is based on those covered by the TIFF file format for Internet fax and by Group 3 facsimile, and a companion document describes the relationship and mapping between this schema and Group 3 fax capabilities.

The document defines its own terms. An extended Internet fax system is any software, device or combination of them that conforms to the specification for Extended Facsimile Using Internet Mail. A capability exchange is any transfer of information between communicating systems used to indicate system capabilities and so determine the form of the data transferred, and it covers both one-way and two-way transfers. Capability identification is a particular form of capability exchange in which a receiving system provides capability information to a sending system. A capability description is a collection of data presented in some format that describes the capabilities of some communicating entity, and it may exist separately from any specific exchange mechanism.

The document is organised in three parts. Section 2 gives the overall syntax for fax feature descriptions, by reference to the media feature registration and syntax documents. Section 3 enumerates the feature tags that extended Internet fax systems are expected to recognise and process, according to their capabilities. Appendix A holds the registrations for the media features specific to fax, for which no applicable registration already exists, in the form prescribed by the registration procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: A fax system has to describe what it can do before a fax is sent, and the description has to mean the same thing on both sides. This document supplies the vocabulary for that, reusing the general media feature machinery rather than inventing a fax-only one. It also does not specify how the description travels; that is left to the mechanisms described elsewhere.

sections.title: The Feature Schema Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax for the fax feature schema is described by the syntax for describing media feature sets, which in turn calls upon media feature tags that may be registered according to the registration procedure.

Media feature registration provides a base vocabulary of features that correspond to media handling capabilities, and the feature set syntax provides a mechanism and format for combining them to describe combinations of features. This document indicates the features that may be associated with extended Internet fax systems.

A feature set is written as a parenthesised expression. The operator & means that all the features inside it must be present, and the operator | means that any one of the alternatives will do. A feature tag is written as a name and a value, and a list of acceptable values is written in square brackets. So a description such as a device that handles either 200 dots per inch at the 200/100 ratio or 300 dots per inch square is written with the two alternatives joined by the vertical bar, and each alternative is a conjunction of features. The examples in Section 4 use exactly this form.
sections.plainLanguage: The syntax is a small language for describing capabilities. A feature is a name and a value, such as the resolution. A parenthesised group joined by and means all of them are needed; a group joined by or means any one will do; square brackets list the values that are acceptable. A whole capability description is one such expression.

sections.title: The Feature Tags
sections.content:
The feature tags in this section are those an extended Internet fax system is expected to recognise its ability or non-ability to handle. A tag in the list does not mean the system has that capability: the system must recognise the tag and deal with it according to the capabilities it does have. A system is not prevented from recognising and offering additional feature tags. The list is a basic vocabulary that all extended Internet fax systems can use consistently, and if an unrecognised or unused tag is received, the feature set matching rule operates so that the tag is effectively ignored.

  • size-x and size-y indicate a rendered document size in inches, given as rational numbers greater than zero. Where the size is measured in millimetres, a conversion factor of 10/254 may be applied to get an exact inch-based value.
  • dpi gives the horizontal resolution and dpi-xyratio the ratio between the two axes. If the ratio is present and not equal to 1, the horizontal resolution is the dpi value and the vertical resolution is the dpi value divided by the ratio, so the basic Group 3 fax resolution of 200 by 100 dots per inch is written as dpi 200 with a ratio of 200/100. For an MRC document the complete set of usable resolutions is listed, with two restrictions: 100 dpi can be used only with multi-level images, and any multi-level image resolution must be an integral sub-multiple of the applicable mask resolution.
  • ua-media names the media, with values such as screen, screen-paged, stationery, transparency, envelope, envelope-plain and continuous.
  • paper-size takes A4, A3, B4, letter or legal.
  • color gives a broad indication of colour handling: Binary, Limited, Mapped, Grey or Full.
  • color-levels, color-space, color-illuminant and the CIELAB tags qualify the colour model further, as described in the next section.
  • image-file-structure says how the coded data is wrapped: TIFF, TIFF-limited, TIFF-minimal, TIFF-MRC or TIFF-MRC-limited. image-coding says how the image data is coded: MH, MR, MMR, JBIG or JPEG, and image-coding-constraint says how that coding is constrained for a particular environment, with JBIG-T85 for bi-level, JBIG-T43 for multi-level and JPEG-T4E. JBIG-stripe-size gives the number of scan lines in each stripe, and image-interleave says whether the image is interleaved by stripe or by plane. color-subsampling is either 1:1:1 for no subsampling or 4:1:1.
  • MRC-mode says whether mixed raster content is available: a zero value means it is not, and a non-zero value gives the maximum available MRC mode number. MRC-max-stripe-size gives the maximum number of scan lines in each MRC stripe.

The document notes that specifying the image file structure alone is not normally enough to describe a recipient's capabilities, and the general rule is that sufficient detail should be provided to exclude any unsupported features. For extended Internet fax, the image file structure and the image coding should always be specified.
sections.plainLanguage: The tags cover the practical questions: how big is the page, how fine is the resolution, what colour, what coding, what file structure, and how the image is laid out in stripes. A system is expected to understand all of them, whether or not it can do them, so that a description from another system can be read and compared.

sections.title: The Colour Model
sections.content:
The model for image handling, for colour and for non-colour, is described from the receiver's point of view, and a similar model operates in the opposite direction for a scan and send perspective. The raw bit stream is a stream of coded bits. Step A is image coding and decoding, with MH, MR, MMR, JPEG and JBIG among the coders. The result is pixel values, a single numeric value per picture element that designates the colour of that element. Step B maps pixel values to colour values, where a colour value has a separate numeric value for each colour component, such as L*, a* and b* in the CIELAB case. Step C relates the colour values to a physical colour, which involves interpreting the colour value with respect to a colour model such as RGB, L*a*b*, CMY or CMYK and a colour space, which is typically recipient-dependent. The end is the physical rendition, a colour value physically realised on a display, printer or other device.

Many variables can be applied at each stage, and any may matter for meaningful handling of an image. The framework is meant to allow capability description at a range of granularity: feature tags that correspond to implied, don't care or unknown values may simply be omitted from a description.

Grey-scale and bi-level images are handled as a special case with a one-component colour model. The color-levels tag gives the number of distinct values for each picture element and applies to all but bi-level images, for which a value of 2 is implied. The color-space tag is used mainly with Mapped and Full colour, and two kinds of colour space are distinguished: device-dependent spaces, named Device-RGB, Device-CMY and Device-CMYK, and calibrated spaces, which presume a rendering system calibrated with respect to an indicated definition and able to process device-independent colour information. A receiver should indicate any device colour space capability it has in addition to any calibrated spaces it supports, and a calibrated space should be used when precise colour matching is required without specific knowledge of the receiving system.

The color-illuminant tag indicates a CIE illuminant, using the same general form as Group 3 fax, with values D50, D65, D75, SA, SC, F2, F7 and F11, or a token of the form CTnnnn where nnnn is a colour temperature in Kelvins, so CT7500 means 7500K. The document notes that in practice the only value likely to be specified is D50, the default illuminant for Group 3 fax.

The CIELAB-L-depth, CIELAB-a-depth and CIELAB-b-depth tags give the number of different values possible for the L*, a* and b* components, and are significant only when colours are represented in a CIELAB space. Colour depth values relate to the representation of colour values rather than the resolution of a scanning or rendering device, so a value of 256 is asserted even if the receiving device can render only 100 distinct luminance values. The CIELAB-x-min and CIELAB-x-max tags give the colour gamut, that is, the range of colour values used or rendered, and a gamut may be indicated in CIELAB terms even when the colours are represented in some other space.
sections.plainLanguage: Colour is handled in three steps: the coded bits are decoded into one number per pixel, those numbers are mapped to one number per colour component, and those components are turned into a colour on the device. The tags describe each step, so a receiver can say whether it can reproduce the whole range the sender has, or only part of it.

sections.title: Example Capability Descriptions
sections.content:
The examples reflect the level of detail used for capability identification in Group 3 facsimile.

The simple mode system uses the minimal black and white TIFF structure, MH coding, A4 paper and stationery media, at either 204 dots per inch with a ratio between 204/98 and 204/196, or 200 dots per inch with a ratio between 200/100 and 1. The high-end black-and-white system adds JBIG bi-level coding with a 128-line stripe and a T.85 constraint, and allows letter, A4 and B4 paper and 300 dots per inch. The grey-scale system extends that with multi-level images, requiring equal horizontal and vertical resolution for them, and describing colour with CIELAB, 256 levels, the D50 illuminant and a lightness range from 0 to 100. The full-colour JPEG example adds 24-bit colour with 16777216 levels and a CIELAB gamut, and allows colour subsampling of 1:1:1 or 4:1:1. The full-colour with JPEG and JBIG example adds limited CMY(K) and RGB colour and 16-bit mapped colour using JBIG coding.

The last example shows how matching works. A receiver is described as accepting 200, 300 or 400 dots per inch, black and white only, A4 or B4 paper, and MH, MR or JBIG coding. The sender has three versions of the document: A4 high resolution black and white, B4 low resolution black and white, and A4 high resolution colour. The three are combined with a logical OR into one composite description, and that is matched against the receiver's description to give the result: the colour version is dropped, because the receiver can handle neither mapped colour nor JPEG coding; the high-resolution version must be sent with JBIG, because that is the only coding the receiver accepts that the sender has at 300 dots per inch; the low-resolution version can be sent with either MH or MR; and the paper sizes are carried over from the document versions. The matching rules also preserve the receiver's constraints on media even though the sender never mentioned that tag. When matching an MRC document description, the description of each component sub-image must match the capabilities of the intended receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how a description is written for a simple machine, a fast black-and-white machine, a grey-scale machine and two colour machines, and then how the sender's and receiver's descriptions are compared. The comparison keeps the best format both sides can do: the colour version is dropped when the receiver cannot take it, and the coding is chosen from the ones both sides have.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Appendix A repeats the descriptions of the feature tags introduced by RFC 2531, with some small revisions. These have been registered in the IETF tree according to the media feature tag registration procedure, so they are subject to the IETF consensus policies of RFC 2434. Section A.5 of the appendix introduces one new feature tag, color-illuminant, to be registered the same way, for which an ASN.1 identifier should be assigned and replaced in the body of the registration.
sections.plainLanguage: The tags are registered with IANA in the same tree as the other media features, so they are subject to the usual IETF process. One new tag, color-illuminant, is added by this document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The points raised here are in addition to the general security considerations for extended Internet fax and those discussed in the media feature and Group 3 fax documents.

Negotiation mechanisms reveal information about one party to other parties. That may raise privacy concerns, and it may allow a malicious party to make better guesses about the presence of specific security holes. Most of these concerns are about capability information getting into the hands of someone who may abuse it. This document specifies capabilities that help a sender to determine what image characteristics the recipient can process, and not mechanisms for their publication, so implementers and users should take care that the mechanisms they employ ensure that capabilities are revealed only to appropriate persons, systems and agents.

The first specific threat is unsolicited bulk mail: if it is known that a recipient can process certain types of images, they may be targeted by bulk mailers who want to send such images.
sections.plainLanguage: Answering the question what can you handle tells the other side something about you, and the document asks that the mechanism used to exchange it reveal capabilities only to the people who should see them. It names one concrete abuse: a sender who knows a recipient handles a particular kind of image can flood them with mail of that kind.

viz.caption: THE FIVE LEVELS OF COLOUR CAPABILITY

cells: Blank and white, or other bi-level capability. No further tags are needed.
A small number of distinct fixed colours, such as a highlight printer. Use color-levels to say how many.
Pixel colour values mapped in a specifiable way to a multi-component colour space.
